ideas: Authorisation: deciding what you're allowed to do
Both together keep the right people on the right data

phrases.phrase: what this means for you is
phrases.meaning: links the idea to the listener's benefit

phrases.phrase: two sides of the same coin
phrases.meaning: two closely connected parts of one thing

learn.explain: These two words sound similar and are often confused. Authentication answers the question "who are you?". It is the login step: a password, a code on your phone, a fingerprint, or signing in with your company Google or Microsoft account. Authorisation answers "what are you allowed to do?". After the system knows who you are, it checks your permissions: a sales rep can see their own customers, a manager can see the whole team, an admin can change settings. Authentication always comes first. Many security problems happen when authentication is strong but authorisation is too generous, so people can see data they shouldn't. In enterprise projects, customers care a lot about connecting to their existing login system.
points: Authentication = who you are (login). Authorisation = what you can do (permissions).
Authentication comes first; authorisation is checked on every action.
Good practice: give people the minimum access they need for their job.
learn.analogy: Think of it like a hotel. At reception you show your passport, and they check you are really you: that's authentication. Then they give you a key card that opens only your room and the gym, not other guests' rooms or the staff office: that's authorisation.

mistakes: Using the two words as if they mean the same thing.
Saying "we have login, so it's secure" and ignoring permissions.
Listing protocols (OAuth, SAML) instead of explaining the two questions.

model: There are really two questions here: who are you, and what are you allowed to do? Authentication is the first one. It's how you prove who you are, with a password, a code on your phone, or your company login. Authorisation is the second one: once the system knows it's you, what you're allowed to do. Think of it like checking into a hotel. At reception, you show your passport and they check it's really you. That's authentication. Then they give you a key card that opens your room and the gym, but not other guests' rooms or the staff office. That's authorisation. They're two sides of the same coin, and you need both. In your company, that would mean your staff log in with the same company account they already use for email, so nobody needs another password. Then, based on their role, a sales rep can only see their own customers, a team lead sees their team, and only two people in IT are in charge of the settings. What this means for you is that people only see what they need for their job. That protects your customers' data, and it makes your audits much easier.
short: Two questions: who are you, and what are you allowed to do? Authentication is proving who you are, like showing your passport at a hotel. Authorisation is what your key card opens. Your staff will log in with their normal company account, and each role only sees what they need. What this means for you is safer customer data and easier audits.

audience.engineer: For authentication we'll integrate with their Azure AD through SSO, using OIDC, so we never store passwords and offboarding is automatic when IT disables an account. MFA is enforced on their side. Authorisation is the harder part. Their requirement is that reps only see their own accounts, so a simple viewer, editor, admin RBAC isn't enough; we need row-level filtering by owner and by team. I'd map their AD groups to our roles, enforce the checks in the API layer rather than the UI, and log every permission denial. We should also confirm whether the AI assistant inherits the user's permissions when it searches documents, because that's where data leaks usually happen.

followUps.q: What happens when someone leaves the company?
followUps.answer: Because they log in with their company account, the moment your IT team disables that account, they lose access to our system too. There's no separate account to forget about.

followUps.q: Can the AI assistant see everything?
followUps.answer: No, and that's important. The assistant only sees what the person asking is allowed to see. If a sales rep asks a question, it only searches documents that rep already has access to.
You do. We'll suggest a starting set based on what we've seen at similar companies, maybe three or four roles, and your team confirms or changes them. It's easy to adjust later.
